Tithe
TYTH
noun / verb (biblical ethics / stewardship)
Old English teogotha (tenth), from Proto-Germanic *teguntha; the tithe is the tenth part of produce or income, set apart for the support of the Levitical priesthood, the temple, and the poor; Hebrew ma'aser (a tenth), from 'eser (ten); Greek apodekatō (to tithe, to pay a tenth); the practice pre-dates Sinai (Abraham to Melchizedek, Gen 14:20; Jacob's vow, Gen 28:22) and is systematized in the Mosaic law (Lev 27:30–33; Num 18:21–32; Deut 14:22–29)

See also: Tithe

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The tithe is the biblically commanded proportion of ten percent of income set aside for the LORD's house and His servants, rooted in the principle that all things belong to God and that the first portion acknowledges His ownership. Leviticus 27:30 establishes the principle: “A tithe of everything from the land — whether grain from the soil or fruit from the trees — belongs to the LORD; it is holy to the LORD.” The Mosaic legislation developed a multi-tithe system: a Levitical tithe (Num 18:21), a festival tithe (Deut 14:22–26), and a poverty tithe every third year (Deut 14:28–29). Malachi 3:10 presents the tithe in covenantal terms — bringing the whole tithe is a test of God: “See if I will not open the windows of heaven for you and pour out a blessing until it overflows.” Jesus acknowledged the practice without condemning it, though He rebuked tithing used to avoid weightier matters of justice and mercy (Matt 23:23): “these you should have done without neglecting the other.” Paul does not cite the tithe formula in his New Testament giving instructions but articulates principles that are compatible with and may exceed it: proportional giving, cheerful giving, and systematic giving (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 9:6–8). The Reformed tradition has generally treated the tithe as the biblical floor for giving: a minimum proportion rooted in both pre-Mosaic and Mosaic pattern, with New Covenant generosity expected to exceed it.

Webster 1828 Definition

TITHE: a tenth part of income or produce set apart for God's service; commanded in the Mosaic law (Lev 27:30) and supported by Malachi 3:10; pre-Mosaic precedent in Abraham (Gen 14:20) and Jacob (Gen 28:22); the Reformed tradition treats it as a biblical floor for New Covenant giving, with generosity expected to exceed it.

expand to see more

TITHE. n. [A.S. teogotha, a tenth.] The tenth part of anything; specifically, the tenth part of the annual produce of lands and labor, set apart for the support of the clergy or for religious purposes.

Webster (1828): “The tenth part of anything; but appropriately, the tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy for their support.” The ecclesiastical application (support of the ministry) is the primary purpose in both Old and New Testament contexts: the Levites received tithes because they had no inheritance in the land (Num 18:21); the NT parallel is the minister's right to financial support from the congregation (1 Cor 9:14; Gal 6:6).

Three Mosaic tithes: (1) the Levitical tithe (Num 18:21–32) — ten percent of annual produce to support the Levites; (2) the festival tithe (Deut 14:22–26) — ten percent brought to Jerusalem for celebration before the LORD; (3) the triennial poor-tithe (Deut 14:28–29) — the third-year tithe set aside for the Levite, sojourner, orphan, and widow. Some calculate the total Mosaic tithe burden at approximately 23 percent.

New Covenant transition: the debate whether the tithe is a moral obligation or a shadow of the Mosaic ceremonial system that has passed is a live intra-Reformed discussion. The majority position in Reformed and Baptist confessional churches treats the tithe as a moral minimum grounded in the pre-Mosaic pattern (Abraham, Jacob), with the ceremonial regulations of the three-tithe system abolished. Systematic, proportional giving (1 Cor 16:2) is the NT pattern; ten percent is the historic biblical benchmark.

The prosperity-gospel corruption of Malachi 3:10 must be distinguished from the genuine covenantal principle: Malachi's promise is to the covenant community, not a vending-machine guarantee of material return; the “blessing” is primarily the continuation of covenant provision for the community's ministry and the poor, not personal financial multiplication.

Key Scripture

Mal 3:10 — "Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, so that there may be food in My house — and test Me now in this," says the LORD of hosts, "if I will not open for you the windows of heaven, and pour out for you a blessing until it overflows."

Lev 27:30 — "Every tithe of the land, whether grain from the fields or fruit from the trees, belongs to the LORD and is holy to the LORD."

Matt 23:23 — "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites — because you pay tithe of mint and dill and cummin, and have neglected the weightier provisions of the Law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. But these are the things you should have done — without neglecting the others."

2 Cor 9:7 — "Each one must do just as he has purposed in his heart — not grudgingly or under compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver."

Modern Corruption

Prosperity-gospel teaching weaponizes the tithe as a financial mechanism to guarantee material return; antinomian evangelicalism dismisses the tithe entirely as Mosaic ceremony; both distort biblical stewardship by detaching giving from covenant faithfulness and God's ownership of all things.

expand to see more

The prosperity gospel's handling of Malachi 3:10 is perhaps the most damaging misreading in contemporary American church life. Kenneth Hagin, Kenneth Copeland, Creflo Dollar, and the broader Word of Faith movement have taught that tithing activates a divine financial multiplication mechanism: give ten percent, receive God's guaranteed financial return. The verse is treated as a personal investment formula rather than a covenantal call to covenant fidelity. The manipulation is compounded when tithing is linked to protecting oneself from a “curse” (Mal 3:9) — tithe to avoid God's curse, tithe to receive material blessing. This reverses the covenant order: the tithe expresses prior trust in God's faithfulness; it is not the mechanism that activates that faithfulness. Malachi's accusation was that Israel had been “robbing God” (3:8) — not paying what was already owed — not that they had missed a financial leverage opportunity.

Antinomian evangelicalism, by contrast, dismisses the tithe as part of the obsolete Mosaic ceremonial system, concluding that no fixed giving percentage applies in the New Covenant. The result is often giving far below ten percent, justified by appeals to “grace giving” and the voluntary character of New Covenant generosity. The error is the selective application of the Mosaic-ceremonial abolition argument: the pre-Mosaic precedents of Abraham and Jacob (Gen 14:20; 28:22) ground the ten-percent principle before Sinai, placing it in the same category as creational ordinances that the New Covenant does not abolish. Moreover, the New Testament's giving instructions (2 Cor 8–9) move in the direction of greater generosity relative to the Mosaic baseline, not lesser.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ma'aser (tenth), from 'eser (ten); Old English teogotha; pre-Mosaic precedent (Abraham, Jacob), Mosaic systematization (Levitical/festival/poor tithes), and New Covenant proportional generosity as the biblical arc of the doctrine.

expand to see more

Hebrew ma'aser — a tenth; from 'eser (ten); the arithmetic simplicity of the fraction is part of its memorability: one part in ten, set apart as the LORD's; the first fruits and the tithe together signal that all belongs to God and the worshiper returns a designated portion as covenant acknowledgment

Abraham to Melchizedek (Gen 14:20) — the first tither in Scripture is Abraham, who gave Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils of battle; the act predates Sinai by four centuries and is interpreted in Hebrews 7 as honoring the higher priesthood — a pre-Mosaic indication that the ten-percent principle is not ceremonially bounded

Jacob's vow (Gen 28:22) — “of all that You give me, I will surely give a tenth to You”; a voluntary but specific proportional commitment made before the Mosaic law; again pre-Sinaitic, grounding the tithe in personal covenant relationship with God

Levitical tithe (Num 18:21–24) — the theological rationale for the tithe in the Mosaic system: the Levites received tithes in place of a land inheritance; the tithing congregation was the means of God's provision for those who served at the altar; in the New Covenant, this translates to the congregation's support of its ministers (1 Cor 9:13–14)

2 Cor 9:6–8 — the New Covenant giving principles: he who sows sparingly reaps sparingly; give as each has decided in the heart; not grudgingly or under compulsion; God loves a cheerful giver; these principles do not abolish the tithe-percentage as a reference point but place it within a larger posture of joyful generosity

Usage

"Pastoral teaching on stewardship should ground the tithe in theology before addressing the finances: everything belongs to the LORD (Ps 24:1), the tithe acknowledges this ownership, and proportional giving is the New Covenant pattern that uses the ten-percent benchmark as a floor. The congregation that understands God's ownership is more likely to give generously than one that is simply told a percentage. John Piper's approach — that the New Covenant believer should not be asking “how little can I give?” but “how much can I invest in the kingdom?” — captures the spirit of 2 Corinthians 8–9."

"The support of elders and ministry staff is the primary New Covenant application of the Levitical-tithe principle. The congregation that withholds adequate financial support from its pastor is violating the principle that the laborer is worthy of his wages (1 Tim 5:18) and that the one who sows spiritual things is entitled to reap material things (1 Cor 9:11). The pastor who is financially stressed is a pastor whose ministry is compromised. Tithes directed to the local church are the primary means of remedying this."

"Generosity beyond the tithe — freewill offerings, special gifts, support of missions and mercy ministries — is the positive expression of New Covenant freedom. The tithe is the floor; the ceiling is the totality of what God has entrusted to the steward. The wealthy believer is not merely a bigger tither; they are a more accountable steward of proportionally greater resources. Luke 12:48 applies: “to whom much is given, much will be required.”"
